title: Mandodari's lament
hook: Ravana's queen weeps; even the villain is mourned

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last arrow, the hymn to the sun, and Ravana falling from his chariot. Your line was it ends. Did you look up once? Day sixty-seven.

When a notorious person dies, the internet celebrates. The jokes arrive within minutes. And somewhere, off-camera, there's a woman sitting on a kitchen floor who has just lost her husband. The war is over. The monkeys are cheering. Ravana lies on the battlefield. And out through the gates of Lanka come the women of the palace, weeping, running to his body. At the front of them is his chief queen. Mandodari. And the Ramayana, a story that spent weeks building Ravana up as the enemy, stops everything to let her speak.
screen: `THE JOKES ARRIVE IN MINUTES.` → `THE WOMEN RUN FROM THE GATES.` → `THE STORY LETS HER SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Mandodari is the daughter of Maya, the great architect of the demons, and in the tradition she is wise and good. In the tradition, she begged Ravana to send Sita back. He wouldn't listen. Now she kneels by his body and grieves, and Valmiki gives her lament room. She remembers his greatness: the king who conquered the gods, who made the worlds tremble. She can't believe he's lying in the dust. She tells him, in effect: I warned you. Your desire for another man's wife is what killed you. And in the same breath, she weeps for him with her whole heart. She doesn't pretend he was innocent. She doesn't pretend she didn't love him. Both are true at once. Then Rama does something just as striking. Vibhishana, Ravana's brother, hesitates to perform the funeral rites: why honor a man who did such wrong? And Rama tells him, in Valmiki's telling, that hostility ends at death. The fight is over. He was your brother. Give him his rites. And Ravana is cremated with the honors of a king. That's hard to sit with. Every villain was somebody's son, somebody's husband, somebody's father. The Ramayana doesn't let you cheer at a funeral. A traditional Sanskrit verse names five honored women, the panchakanya, and Mandodari is one of them, with Ahalya, Draupadi and Tara. Her grief is honored, not mocked. Compassion for the fallen doesn't excuse anything. It just refuses to forget that someone loved him.
screen: `MANDODARI BEGGED HIM TO LISTEN.` · `I WARNED YOU. AND I LOVED YOU.` · `HOSTILITY ENDS AT DEATH.` · `EVERY VILLAIN WAS SOMEBODY'S.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of someone who fell. Someone in the news, someone in your family, someone who did real harm and paid for it. Don't excuse what they did. Just picture, for a moment, the person who loved them. A mother. A husband. A child. What are they feeling tonight? Let that sit next to everything else you know. You can hold both: what was wrong, and the grief. If you pray, you can hold those mourners in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Mandodari's lament. Ravana's queen, kneeling by his body, grieving the king she warned and still loved.
Your line: someone loved him. Today, before you join in on anyone's downfall, remember there's someone at home who's grieving. Day sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Mandodari is remembered in Hindu tradition as a wise and virtuous queen and is named in a well-known Sanskrit verse listing five revered women, the panchakanya, traditionally recited in the morning.

original.note: Sanskrit: Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, daughter of Maya the architect.

trapdoor: what you thought: the villain dies and everyone cheers.
what it means: the story stops to let the villain's wife grieve, and the hero insists on his funeral rites.
what a scholar hears: Rama's words that hostility ends at death, and Mandodari's place among the five revered women, the panchakanya.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the lament of Ravana's wives and Mandodari; Rama and Vibhishana on the funeral rites, roughly sargas 109–113)
the panchakanya verse (Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita or Kunti, Tara, Mandodari)

notes: Mandodari's lament and Rama's 'hostility ends at death' (the 'maranantani vairani' verse, as remembered) are paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm references.
The teach names Ahalya, Draupadi and Tara from the panchakanya verse and leaves out the fifth, which varies by recension (Sita or Kunti). Confirm.
Mandodari as daughter of Maya (Mayasura) the architect: confirm.
The prayer line in the practice is optional ('if you pray'); no new prayer is written.

Editor review (days 57–75): 'more than once she begged' is now 'in the tradition' (her pleading is fullest in later tellings such as Tulsidas; confirm Valmiki); cut the superlative 'one of the most moving passages'; replaced the stock turn; panchakanya line no longer says 'many Hindus'.
